title: Polymer clay aurora blend earrings
subtitle: Gradient disc earrings blended from two or three polymer clay colours
excerpt: These drop earrings are cut from thin sheets of polymer clay blended from two or three colours so the hues merge across the disc. The gradient: known in polymer clay as a Skinner blend: gives each pair a soft aurora effect. The clay sets in a domestic oven. No kiln required.
sourceNotes: Skinner blend technique documented as a polymer clay method developed in the 1990s; technique references derived from polymer clay practice. Earring construction derived from first principles.

glossaryTerms.definition: A polymer clay gradient technique in which two or more colour triangles are folded and rolled repeatedly until the colours merge smoothly from one to the next.
Warming and kneading polymer clay until it is soft and pliable, which distributes the plasticiser evenly and makes the cured piece stronger.

content.text: Polymer clay earrings are a good introduction to the material: the pieces are small, the oven cure is short (15 to 30 minutes at 130°C), and the margin for error is wider than in full sculptural work. The gradient technique here: a
Skinner blend
: blends two or three clay colours across a sheet so the transition is smooth rather than hard-edged. The cured discs are lightweight and hold ear wires without cracking.

Polymer clay sets in a domestic oven at 110 to 130°C for 15 to 30 minutes. Use a dedicated oven liner or a ceramic tile as a baking tray: do not share with food-preparation cookware. The cured clay is a hard plastic, not a true ceramic. It is not food-safe, not microwave-safe, and not dishwasher-safe.
What you'll need

Two contrasting blocks of polymer clay: approximately 15 g each. A pair of ear wires with a loop (available from craft suppliers). A 3 cm round cutter or a small circle template cut from card. A baking tray lined with ceramic tile or dedicated baking paper.
Conditioning the clay
Polymer clay must be conditioned before use. Cold, fresh-from-the-packet clay is stiff and may crack when bent.
Conditioning

: kneading and folding the clay until it is warm and pliable: distributes the plasticiser through the body. A fully conditioned block bends without cracking and rolls into a thin sheet without tearing.

Cut 15 g from each colour block. Knead each piece between the palms for two minutes, then roll it into a log and fold it in half repeatedly until the surface is smooth and the clay flexes without cracking.
Roll each conditioned block into a flat sheet about 2 mm thick using the rolling pin on a smooth non-porous surface.

Cut each sheet into a right-angle triangle with the longest edge the same length as the short side of the other triangle. Place the two triangles side by side with the long edges touching, so the colours meet diagonally.

Roll the combined piece flat: the colours will begin to merge at the edge. Fold the sheet in half with the grain (always fold so the same edge meets the same edge) and roll flat again. Repeat 15 to 20 times. After 20 folds and rolls, the colour transition should be smooth with no hard line between them.
Roll the gradient sheet to a final thickness of 2 mm. Cut two 3 cm circles from the area where the gradient is most pronounced.
Pierce a small hole at the top of each disc with the needle tool, 3 mm from the edge. This is the loop for the ear wire.
Place the discs on a ceramic tile or oven liner. Bake at 130°C for 20 minutes. Allow to cool completely on the tile before handling: hot polymer clay is soft and will dent under finger pressure.
Thread the ear wire loop through the pierced hole and close the loop with jewellery pliers.
Care

Polymer clay is a hard plastic after curing: it does not absorb moisture and does not need sealing. The surface can be lightly buffed with a soft cloth for a low sheen. Store in a soft pouch to prevent scratching. Do not leave in direct sunlight for extended periods; polymer can yellow slightly with sustained UV exposure.
Variations
Three-colour blend: lay three triangles in sequence and fold and roll as above: the transitions go colour A to B to C across the sheet.
Use a teardrop or half-moon cutter instead of a circle for a different earring silhouette.
Roll the sheet to 3 mm and stamp with a texture before cutting the circles: the gradient shows through the texture pattern.

rows.problem: Colour gradient has a hard line, not a smooth blend
rows.cause: Not enough fold-and-roll cycles; clay too stiff to merge
rows.fix: Fully condition both colours before blending. Increase to 25 to 30 fold-and-roll cycles.

rows.problem: Discs crack or warp in the oven
rows.cause: Clay not fully conditioned; oven temperature too high or too fast to reach temperature
rows.fix: Condition thoroughly. Use an oven thermometer to confirm your oven's actual temperature: many domestic ovens run 10 to 15°C hot.

rows.cause: Hole too close to the edge; hole too small
rows.fix: Pierce the hole at least 3 mm from the edge. Widen the hole slightly before baking by rotating the needle tool in a circle.
